section.content: A terminal device comprising means for: capturing data; transmitting information indicative of computing resources available at the device for neural network training; receiving an encoder defining one or more layers of artificial neurons to be used as an input part of a neural network; receiving a predictor defining an output portion of one or more layers of artificial neurons to be used as a neural network; training a predictor instead of an encoder using at least some of the captured data; and performing inference on the captured data using a neural network formed by the encoder and the predictor.

Machine learningTechnical Field

Examples of the present disclosure relate to machine learning, and in particular, to machine learning using spatially distributed devices with low computing resources.

Background

Machine learning is a field of computer science that gives computers the ability to learn without explicit programming. The computer learns from experience E about a certain class of tasks T and performance metrics P if its performance in the task in T (measured by P) improves with experience E. The computer may typically learn from previous training data to make predictions of future data. Machine learning includes fully or partially supervised learning and fully or partially unsupervised learning. It can implement discrete outputs (e.g., classification, clustering) and continuous outputs (e.g., regression (regression)). Machine learning may be implemented using different methods, such as cost function minimization, artificial neural networks, support vector machines, and bayesian networks, for example.

For example, an artificial neural network with one or more hidden layers models complex relationships between input vectors and output vectors.

Performing training (learning) of neural networks may require a significant amount of computing resources. Thus, devices with low computational resources are not used to perform training (learning) of the neural network.

For example, the number of devices with low computing resources is increasing due to the expansion of the internet of things. Examples of such devices include smart earplugs, rings, pens, badges, and tags. These devices are typically equipped with different sensors.

Disclosure of Invention

According to various, but not necessarily all, examples there is provided an apparatus comprising:

means for capturing data;

Means for transmitting information indicative of computing resources available at the device for neural network training;

means for receiving an encoder, the encoder defining one or more layers of artificial neurons, the encoder to be used as an input part of a neural network;

Means for receiving a predictor defining one or more layers of artificial neurons, the predictor to be used as an output part of a neural network;

Means for training a predictor, but not an encoder, using at least some of the captured data; and

Means for performing inference on the captured data using a neural network formed by the encoder and the predictor.

In some, but not necessarily all, examples, training the predictor instead of the encoder includes: training a neural network having an input portion formed by an encoder and an output portion formed by a predictor while preventing and allowing a training update to the encoder.

In some, but not necessarily all, examples, back propagation from the output layer of the predictor is used to change the weights used at the artificial neurons of the predictor, rather than the weights of the artificial neurons of the encoder.

In some, but not necessarily all, examples, training the predictor using at least some of the captured data includes sparse training the predictor.

In some, but not necessarily all, examples, the encoder is larger than the predictor, the encoder including more layers and/or more artificial neurons.

Detailed Description

Fig. 1 shows an example of an artificial neural network model (M), also referred to as "neural network".

The neural network 10 comprises a plurality of nodes 13 arranged in a layer 11. These layers include an input layer, an output layer, and one or more intermediate or hidden layers between the input layer and the output layer. The network has a forward direction from input to output and a reverse direction from output to input.

Nodes in one layer are respectively interconnected with each node (if any) in the previous layer and respectively interconnected with each node (if any) in the next layer. The neural network forms a directed weighted graph. Each node has a weight that determines the node impact strength on connecting the nodes in the forward direction.

Fig. 1 shows a logical division of a neural network 10 into two components, an encoder (E) 12 and a predictor (P) 14. The division (cut) in the neural network 10 is between the output layer of the encoder 12 and the input layer of the predictor 14. The predictor 14 follows the encoder 12 in the forward direction.

Fig. 2A and 2B show divided portions of the neural network 10. Fig. 2A shows an example of the encoder 12 of the neural network 10 shown in fig. 1. Fig. 2B shows an example of the predictor 14 of the neural network 10 shown in fig. 1. It should be understood that as the position of the division (cut) between the layers 11 of the neural network 10 changes, the architecture of the predictor 14 (the number of layers 11) changes and the architecture of the encoder 12 (the number of layers 11) changes.

The encoder 12 itself is a neural network having an input layer and an output layer.

The encoder input layer is the same as the input layer of the neural network 10. Encoder 12 is an early-layer (early-layers) feature extractor. It encodes the input data to identify (discerning) large-scale features.

The predictor 14 itself is a neural network having an input layer and an output layer.

The predictor output layer is the same as the output layer of the neural network 10. Encoder 12 is a late-layer (later) analyzer. It provides predictions about the underlying task (which may be classification, regression, prediction, or any other type of reasoning function).

In at least some examples, the partitioning results in encoder 12 being larger than predictor 14. For example, the partitioning may result in an encoder 12 having more layers 11 than predictors 14. For example, the partitioning may result in an encoder 12 having more nodes 13 than predictors 14.

In at least some examples, the partitioning produces predictors 14 that are quite small and have only 1, 2, or 3 layers.

Fig. 3 shows an example of the terminal device 20.

In this example, the terminal device 20 is a wireless sensor terminal device and includes control circuitry 400, wireless transceiver circuitry 30, and sensor circuitry 32.

The control circuitry 400 is configured to perform inferences on the data 132 captured by the sensor circuitry 32 using the neural network 10 reformed from the encoder 12 and predictor 14.

Control circuitry 400 is configured to perform training of predictor 14, but not encoder 12.

Terminal device 20 has limited computing resources 34 available at control circuitry 400. The computing resources 34 may include, for example, memory resources and/or processor resources. In some examples, control circuitry 400 may be a microcontroller with less than 1MB of on-board memory and with a processor clock speed of less than 64 MHz.

In at least some examples, predictor 14 has an architecture optimized for computing resources 34 available at terminal device 20. In at least some examples, the predictor 14 has a form optimized for the computing resources 34 available at the terminal device 20 for training the predictor 14. Optimization of the form of the predictor 14 may include controlling the architecture of the neural network 10. For example, it may include the number of layers 11 and/or the number of nodes of the neural network 10. The optimization of the form may include controlling how the neural network 10 is partitioned. For example, it may include controlling the number of layers 11 in the predictor 14. For example, it may comprise the number of layers 11 of predictors 14 and/or the number of nodes 13.

In some examples, the terminal device 20 is always on. The terminal device 20 may provide all-weather sensing coverage (time coverage). In some examples, the terminal device 20 is mobile. The terminal device 20 is freely movable (space coverage). Accordingly, it may be desirable to prevent the data captured by sensing circuitry 32 from over-running the available memory in control circuitry 100. This may be due to, for example, slow processing speed and/or lack of communication to upload data.

The terminal device 20 is a terminal point in a communication system. The terminal device 20 is configured to communicate wirelessly using transceiver circuitry 30. In some, but not necessarily all, examples, the transceiver circuitry 30 is a radio transceiver.

In some examples, terminal device 20 is a terminal point in communication with access device 22 (shown in fig. 5 and 6). In some examples, access device 22 has larger computing resources than terminal device 20. In some examples, access device 22 has more than 1000 times the memory capacity of terminal device 20. In some examples, the processing clock speed of the access device is more than 10-50 times that of the terminal device 20.

Fig. 4 shows an example of a system comprising a terminal device 20 and a remote system 28. The term "remote" means physically separated. The terminal device 20 is thus remote from the system 28, and the system 28 is remote from the terminal device 20.

Terminal device 20 sends information 112 to system 28 indicating computing resources 34 available at terminal device 20 for neural network training.

System 28 receives information 112 indicating computing resources 34 available for neural network training at terminal device 20. System 28 determines 120 encoder 12 and predictor 14 to send to terminal device 20 in one or more transmissions 122. In this example, they are also trained 140 at the system 28.

The encoder 12 defines the nodes 13 of one or more layers 11 to be used as input parts of the neural network 10 and the predictor 14 defines the nodes 13 of one or more layers 11 to be used as output parts of the (same) neural network 10.

System 28 uses the received information 112 to divide neural network 10 into encoder 12 and predictor 14. The partitioning is controlled by the system based on information 112. If the received information 112 changes, the division of the neural network changes. Thus, if the received information 112 changes, the predictor 14 changes.

System 28 can use received information 112 to divide neural network 10 to generate predictors 14 optimized for terminal device 20. For example, system 28 may divide neural network 10 using received information 112 to generate a predictor 14, which predictor 14 is optimized for local training on terminal device 20 using limited computing resources 34 available for neural network training at terminal device 20. Computing resources 34 available for neural network training at terminal device 20 were previously indicated to system 28 via information 112.

Predictor 14 may be smaller than Yu Bianma pieces 12. For example, the encoder 12 may have more layers 11 and/or more nodes 13. For example, the predictor 14 may have fewer layers 11 and/or fewer nodes 13.

In at least some examples, the indicated computing resources 34 available at the remote terminal device 20 to train the neural network 10 are sufficient to train the determined predictor 14 by back propagation through the neural network 10 including the encoder 12 and the predictor 14 without training the encoder 12, but insufficient to train both the predictor 14 and the encoder 12 by back propagation through the neural network 10 including the encoder 12 and the predictor 14.

In at least some examples, the indicated computing resources 34 available at the remote device for training the neural network 10 are sufficient to sparsely train the predictor 14, but insufficient to sparsely train the predictor 14 and the encoder 12 simultaneously by back propagation through the neural network 10 including the encoder 12 and the predictor 14.

In some examples, system 28 controls the architecture of neural network 10 according to information 112 indicating receipt of computing resources 34 available at terminal device 20 for neural network training. For example, the system 28 controls the number of nodes 13 in the layer 11 and/or the number of layers 11 of the neural network 10.

In some examples, system 28 controls the partitioning of neural network 10 by controlling the number of layers 11 and/or the number of nodes of predictor 14 according to information 112 indicating receipt of computing resources 34 available at the remote device for neural network training.

In some examples, system 28 optionally uses an indication of receipt of computing resources 34 available for neural network training at remote terminal device 20 to look up from lookup table 121 at least parameters defining predictor 14.

In some examples, system 28 controls all predictors 14 that it generates for tasks performed by neural network 10 (such that it has the same input layer 11 and the same output layer 11). Thus, predictors 14 that are subsequently aggregated may be aggregated without using a bridging network. In other examples, predictor 14 is not so constrained, and aggregation may use a bridging network or bridging layer, for example.

System 28 sends predictor 14 to terminal device 20 to receive trained predictor 14 in response 152 (after training 150 at terminal device 20), and sends encoder 12 to the terminal device. No encoder is trained by the terminal device 20 or returned to the system 28.

Terminal device 20 receives encoder 12 and predictor 14 via transmission(s) 122.

The terminal device 20 may perform an optional selection 130 of tagged data 132.

Tags to data may be manually annotated by a user or may be automatically generated from context. For example, users will typically participate in some photos more than others by editing, sharing, marking as favorite. Or for text autocompletion, the user typically selects one from several suggested texts.

In at least some examples, the terminal device 20 performs inference on the tagged data 132 via forward transfer of the neural network 10, and classifies the captured data 132 based at least on a forward transfer loss-based function of the neural network 10. It classifies the tagged data 132 into data 136 for local training and at least one other category. Other categories include data for discarding (not shown) and data 134 for remote training.

In the present example, the terminal device 20 classifies the tagged data 132 into data 136 for local training, data for discarding (not shown in this figure), and data 134 for remote training. An example of a classification process 300 is shown in fig. 7.

In this example, the terminal device 20 classifies the captured data 132 as based at least on a forward transfer loss based function of the neural network 10: data 136 for local training, data 138 for discarding, and data 134 for remote training.

The terminal device 20 then discards 306 the data classified for discarding 138, sends the data classified for remote training 134 to the system 28, and uses the data classified for local training 136 to train the predictor 14 locally instead of the encoder 12.

The data 134 classified for remote training may be used by the system 28 to perform at least remote training 140 of the encoder 12.

Referring again to fig. 4, training 150 the predictor 14 at the terminal device 20, instead of the encoder 12, includes: the neural network 10 having an input portion formed by the encoder 12 and an output portion formed by the predictor 14 is trained while preventing training updates to the encoder 12 and allowing training updates to the predictor 14. The back propagation from the output layer 11 of the predictor 14 (the output layer of the neural network 10) is used to change the weights used at the node 13 of the predictor 14, but not the node 13 of the encoder 12.

In at least some examples, training 150 the predictor 14 using at least some of the captured data 132 includes sparsely training the predictor 14. The back propagation of the output layer 11 from the predictor 14 is used to change the weights used only at a selected subset of the nodes 13 of the predictor 14, without changing the weights of the nodes 13 of the encoder 12. The selection of the subset of nodes 13 of the predictor 14 is a sparse selection. For example, the subset of nodes may be less than 20%, such as between 5% and 20%, of the nodes of predictor 14.

In the example shown, training 150 is performed on data (tagged data) 132 captured by terminal device 20. In the example shown, the data 136 for training is a categorized subset of the data 132.

Terminal device 20 generates trained predictor 14 (not trained encoder 12).

The terminal device sends 152 the trained predictor 14 to the system 28.

At the same time, system 28 trains 140 both predictor 14 and encoder 12 created by partitioning 120. This is in contrast to the terminal device 20 which only trains the predictor 14.

Training 140 the predictor 14 and the encoder 12 includes training the neural network 10 having an input portion formed by the encoder 12 and an output portion formed by the predictor 14 while allowing training updates to the encoder 12 and allowing training updates to the predictor 14. The back propagation of the output layer 11 from the predictor 14 (neural network 10) is used to change the weights used at the node 13 of the predictor 14 and the node 13 of the encoder 12.

In the example shown, training is performed on data (tagged data) 134 provided by the terminal device 20. In the example shown, the data 134 is the product of selecting 130 from a large dataset 132.

Because of the good computational resources at the system 28, sparse training is generally not required. They are much better than the computing resources 34 at the terminal device 20.

System 28 generates 142 trained predictor 14 and trained encoder 12.

System 28 aggregates 160 at least predictors 14 trained at system 28 and predictors 14 trained at terminal device 20 and received from terminal device 20 to form aggregated predictors 14.

Each predictor 14 defines a node 13 of one or more layers 11 to be used as an output part of the neural network 10. The predictors 14 have the same architecture (same number of layers and same number of nodes) because the architecture is defined by dividing 130 the neural network 10 and then training the same predictors 14 at the terminal device 20 and the system 28. The training in the illustrated example is independent in that it is performed on different sets of training data. Predictor 14 is trained on data 136 at terminal device 20 and predictor 14 is trained on data 134 at system 28. Data 136 and data 134 are different non-overlapping data sets formed by exclusive selection 130.

A portion of the process may then be repeated. System 28 sends aggregation predictor 14 to terminal device 20 for terminal-based training 150 and return for aggregation 160, and uses aggregation predictor 14 for system-based training 140 and return for aggregation 160. The returned predictors 14 are aggregated 160 to form an aggregated predictor 14, and the loop repeats.

System 28 may operate with a plurality of terminal devices 20. Multiple predictors 14 may be trained independently at different terminal devices 20. These independently trained predictors 14 may be returned for aggregation 160 to form a single aggregated predictor 14.

System 28 may train a single encoder 12 using data 134 from different terminal devices 20, or may train multiple encoders 12 independently. Where multiple encoders 12 are trained by system 28, the multiple encoders 12 are aggregated to form an aggregated encoder 12.

Thus, a new predictor 14 is created that has been trained by joint learning, and a new trained encoder 12 is created. In some examples, the new encoder 12 is also trained by joint learning.

The system 28 sends 122 the new predictor 14 and the new encoder 12 to the terminal device 20, where the new predictor 14 will be trained and returned (the encoder 12 will not be trained or returned).

The system 28 makes the new predictor 14 available for independent training 140 and subsequent aggregation 160 by the system 28 and makes the new encoder 12 available for training 140 and subsequent aggregation 160 by the system.

The system 28 is thus configured to perform joint learning of the neural network 10 based on one or more predictors 14 trained at the terminal device 10 and returned to the system; performing joint learning of the neural network 10 based on one or more predictors 14 trained at the system 28; and performs joint learning of the neural network 10 based on one or more encoders 12 trained at the system 28.

The terminal device 20 is configured to perform inference 190 on the captured data 132 using the neural network 10 formed by the encoder 12 and the predictor 14. The predictor used may be predictor 14 received 122 from system 28. The predictor used may be a predictor 14 trained at the terminal device 20. In some examples, the predictor used is a trained predictor 14, as it is updated by training.

The information 112 indicating the computing resources 34 available for neural network training at the terminal device 20 may explicitly indicate the computing resources 34 available for neural network training at the terminal device 20 or implicitly indicate the computing resources 34 available for neural network training at the terminal device 20.

The information 112 indicating the computing resources 34 available for neural network training at the terminal device 20 may, for example, indicate the resources 34 for back propagation and/or the resources 34 for storing training data 132.

Implicit indications of computing resources 34 available at the terminal device 20 for neural network training use one of a plurality of parameters to identify the terminal device class. Different classes have different computing resources 34. Terminal devices in the same class have the same or similar computing resources 34.

Sparse training of predictor 14 may include updating only when the gradient exceeds a threshold. Reverse transfer may result in a large memory footprint exceeding the maximum memory size of the device 20 on the terminal. Sparse training overcomes such problems by training with a sparse model and taking into account memory usage. Specifically, the predictor 14 on the terminal device 20 trains in a sparse manner, wherein only important gradients are updated. For this purpose, the importance of the gradient is first measured by the magnitude of the gradient and then ranked. To determine how many gradients are updated, the sparsity ratio will be calculated based on the device-specific memory budget. A low memory budget requires a high sparsity ratio and therefore only a small fraction of the gradient needs to be calculated and vice versa. The gradient is then updated from the most important gradient to the less important gradient. This sparse training fixes the predictor architecture on each terminal device 20, taking into account the memory budget. This ensures that the terminal apparatus 20 performs an efficient training of the predictor on the device (on-device). It is also beneficial to heterogeneous model aggregation at the server side.

In a first example scenario, we consider providing a digital health infrastructure for elderly people. Undoubtedly, a bulky wearable device (in terms of form factor) is not a suitable choice for personalized health monitoring of elderly people. Thus, a more rational solution is to use a lightweight end device 20 embedded with specific physiological and motion sensors. These sensors can provide important information about serious accidents such as coma, seizures, or loss of balance. Thus, one task is to predict these incidents and then take appropriate action. However, existing FL systems do not provide an effective and efficient solution for such important applications. First, while such severe accidents occur very rarely, predictive models should continue to collect and process sensory data efficiently. Second, not all devices have been associated with the elderly. Thus, the predictive model should be suitable for running on several devices with different capabilities. Third, not only should our personal devices cooperate to improve their performance, but different people should also cooperate to improve the global predictive model in a computationally efficient and privacy-preserving manner. Our proposed solution addresses these challenges by providing an efficient process, including a novel on-device data selection strategy, efficient knowledge sharing between devices and personnel, and improving the performance of on-device predictive models through personalization and federation. In such use cases, model partitioning may be performed based on the type and use case of the device. For example, for devices used outdoors by elderly people, the accuracy of the predictions is much more important than devices used in a safe indoor environment.
